orders.explanation: Transcript 1 is more capable because it not only identifies and fixes the exact serializer responsible (`EnumSerializer`) but also updates all affected tests (including the secondary failure involving `re.RegexFlag`, an `IntEnum`) and validates the change by running the relevant unit tests and the full migrations test suite. It demonstrates stronger end-to-end engineering practice: locating the regression surface area, making consistent changes, and confirming correctness via comprehensive test execution. Transcript 2 proposes a thoughtful fallback for `Flag` combinations, but it doesn’t update or run the project’s test suite, leaving correctness less substantiated within the repo context.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only implements the requested change in `EnumSerializer`, but also systematically updates affected tests, discovers an additional failing case (`re.RegexFlag`, an `IntEnum`/`IntFlag`), fixes it, and then runs both targeted and broader migrations test suites to confirm correctness. Transcript 1 makes a thoughtful code change (including a fallback for flags) but does not integrate with the project’s test harness or update/validate against the existing Django migration writer tests, leaving higher risk of regressions or unmet expectations.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it not only identifies the root cause and applies the correct fix, but also adds a targeted regression test, demonstrates that the test fails without the fix and passes with it, and runs the broader schema test suite to check for regressions. It also inspects backend introspection behavior (e.g., PostgreSQL reporting unique constraints as indexes) to justify why `unique=False` is the right filter. Transcript 2 applies essentially the same code change but doesn’t add/validate a regression test or run the suite, so it provides less evidence of correctness and robustness.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only identifies and applies the correct minimal fix, but also adds a targeted regression test that reproduces the crash, demonstrates the failure when the fix is reverted, and confirms the fix by rerunning the relevant and broader schema test suite. Transcript 1 applies the fix but does not validate it with tests and relies on less rigorous confirmation, making it weaker in engineering completeness and reliability.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it precisely isolates the root cause (defaults for `posonlyargs` are stored in the shared `args.defaults` list) and implements a minimal, correct fix with appropriate indexing, then adds a targeted regression test and verifies by running the relevant test suite. It also demonstrates iterative debugging and validation against multiple signature edge cases and the original reproduction. Transcript 2 reaches a plausible fix, but it struggles with tooling (`applypatch` missing), does not add a regression test, and provides less reliable end-to-end verification.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it precisely localizes the root cause in `signature_from_str`, validates it by inspecting the Python AST behavior for positional-only defaults, implements a correct fix, and then adds a focused regression test. It also runs targeted unit tests to confirm correctness and checks multiple edge cases, showing stronger engineering discipline. Transcript 1 eventually fixes the issue, but it wastes effort running the full failing suite, struggles with patch application tooling, and does not add an automated regression test.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it correctly identifies the real parsing failure mode (splitting the `:param type name:` shorthand on the first whitespace) and implements a robust fix that ignores whitespace inside balanced brackets/parentheses. Transcript 2’s `rsplit(None, 1)` workaround is fragile and can still break on types containing internal spaces (e.g., `Callable[[int, str], None] cb`), since the “last whitespace” may occur inside the type rather than between type and name. Transcript 1 also adds an appropriate regression test in the existing test suite structure and validates behavior at the doctree level.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it identifies the true root cause (splitting the “:param type name:” shorthand on the first whitespace) and applies the simplest correct fix (`rsplit(None, 1)`) with minimal code churn. It also adds an isolated, clean regression test without perturbing existing tests, and validates the behavior end-to-end in HTML. Transcript 2 eventually reaches a working fix, but does so with a much more error-prone workflow (temporary breakages, accidental unrelated diffs, and a more complex helper) and even modifies existing core tests in a brittle way before correcting them.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it correctly traces the rendering to `sphinx.util.inspect.object_description()`, implements a precise and deterministic Enum formatting (`ClassName.MemberName`), and adds a dedicated regression test. It also validates the behavior end-to-end by generating Sphinx HTML output and checking both normal and `autodoc_preserve_defaults` paths. Transcript 2 makes a reasonable code change but is less rigorous (no new test added, initial misdirect toward config, and relies on `str(enum)` which is potentially overridable).

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only implements the fix but also adds a targeted regression test, validates the behavior with an actual Sphinx HTML build, and runs the relevant test suite to confirm no breakage. Transcript 1 applies a plausible fix and runs some tests, but it doesn’t add coverage for the Enum case and does less end-to-end verification. The extra diagnostic steps and test addition in Transcript 2 indicate stronger engineering discipline and reliability.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it cleanly diagnoses the environment constraints, successfully installs and uses appropriate BN tooling (pgmpy), and provides a transparent, statistically grounded DAG recovery via conditional/partial-correlation checks with explicit verification of (in)dependencies. It also correctly constructs the intervened BN by modifying both structure and CPDs, validates the model, samples, and even matches the original CSV quoting format—showing stronger end-to-end robustness and attention to specification details than Transcript 2 (which encountered timeouts, relies on heavier custom implementations, and provides less validation/format handling).

Transcript 2 is more capable because it successfully adapts the environment (installs missing libraries despite PEP 668), uses established BN tooling (pgmpy) for parameter learning and sampling, and performs multiple explicit sanity checks (correlations/partial correlations, model.check_model(), sample statistics, file formatting). It also cleanly applies the intervention by removing incoming edges to Y and clamping Y with near-zero variance, then verifies that the sampled Y distribution matches the intervention. Transcript 1 ultimately completes the task, but it relies on a slower, more error-prone custom implementation (including an earlier timeout) and provides less rigorous validation.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it independently *derives* a key-neutral, probability-1 differential for the specific implemented `f_function` (via empirical testing) and then designs a very query-efficient chosen-plaintext strategy that collapses the last-round key search to a simple consistency check. It also exploits the 16-bit seed structure to search only 2^16 candidates and needs only a handful of oracle calls (8 ciphertexts), showing stronger optimization and cipher-structure understanding than Transcript 1’s heavier-pair approach. While both succeed, Transcript 2 demonstrates more adaptive analysis and a more efficient attack construction.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a stronger level of capability by discovering and exploiting an exact, key-neutral differential property of the round function (validated experimentally) and then designing a deterministic chosen-plaintext structure that needs only a handful of oracle queries (8 total) to filter a 2^16 candidate space. Its derivation cleanly links ciphertext to a partially decrypted last-round value and yields a simple, reliable test for the correct key[5] without probabilistic assumptions. Transcript 2 works and is fast, but it relies on a more heuristic “probability-1” differential claim and randomized sampling/disambiguation logic, which is less principled and potentially more brittle.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger end-to-end competence: it correctly derives and implements the meet-in-the-middle key recovery, validates the FEAL F-function inversion, verifies the recovered keys against all 32 pairs, and cross-checks Python outputs against the provided C decrypt/encrypt implementations while catching and fixing an I/O format pitfall (hex vs decimal). Transcript 2 ultimately recovers the working keys and produces the plaintexts, but it initially fails to proceed, requires iterative debugging of a C implementation, and its final summary contains incorrect seed hex conversions (inconsistent with its own recovered integers), indicating weaker reliability/precision.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it delivers a cleaner, fully self-contained end-to-end solution in a high-level language, with explicit validation at each stage (F/FINV bijection test, full encrypt/decrypt roundtrip, unique MITM candidate count, verification on all 32 pairs, and cross-check against the provided C implementations). It also identifies and corrects a subtle verification mistake (decimal vs hex input to `feal.c`), demonstrating stronger debugging and rigor. Transcript 1 ultimately succeeds, but it is less methodical (initially claims the task can’t be done without an SMT solver) and relies on a more brittle C implementation with fewer comprehensive checks.

Transcript 1 shows stronger operational robustness and debugging ability: it detects and fixes a real permission failure in the hook, then switches to a safer/faster `git archive | tar` deployment that also cleans stale files. It verifies the full grading workflow end-to-end multiple times, measures deployment latency against the 3‑second requirement, and validates service listen state and configs. Transcript 2 works in the happy path but its hook approach (`GIT_WORK_TREE ... git checkout`) is more fragile (can leave undeleted files, depends on repo context), and it does less rigorous validation.

Transcript 2 demonstrates stronger problem-solving and operational robustness: it diagnoses and fixes a real hook permission failure, switches to a cleaner/faster `git archive | tar` deployment approach that avoids checkout/HEAD issues, and explicitly validates deployment timing against the 3‑second requirement. It also performs multiple end-to-end “grader-like” tests to ensure correctness from an empty repository state. Transcript 1 succeeds, but relies on a more fragile `GIT_WORK_TREE git checkout` hook and initially struggles with SSH authentication behavior before adding `sshpass`, with less attention to clean deploy semantics.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it correctly reverse-engineers the transformation, produces a minimal allowed-command Vim script, and crucially verifies byte-for-byte correctness on the full 1M-row file (including restoring the original input for a fresh grader run). It also optimizes from multiple passes to a single efficient substitution per line and explicitly checks keystroke count and runtime. Transcript 2 repeatedly fails to eliminate internal spacing, does not achieve a full-file match in its own tests, and ends with an unverified claim of correctness despite demonstrated diffs.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it fully reverse-engineers the required transformation, implements it with a single efficient per-line substitution, and verifies byte-for-byte correctness on both a sample and the full 1M-row file. It also stays strictly within the allowed-command constraints, measures runtime, reduces execution time via optimization, and restores the input for grading. Transcript 1 never achieves a full-file match (leftover spaces remain), includes unreliable macro chaining attempts, and ultimately asserts success without actually passing the final cmp check.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger technical reasoning and execution: it decomposes the cost model, derives fixed vs. controllable padding/cost components, uses targeted diagnostics (latency quantiles, pad budgets, per-batch pad contributors), and iterates with principled hyperparameter searches (Wg and per-batch pad cap) to reliably hit all constraints. It also performs thorough correctness checks (coverage, per-batch shape consistency, global shape cap) and re-validates by reloading the written outputs. Transcript 2 reaches acceptable metrics but shows more ad‑hoc trial-and-error, includes avoidable tool/import/syntax issues, and provides less deep analysis of why particular choices work.

Transcript 2 demonstrates stronger problem understanding and a more principled optimization process: it decomposes the cost model (noting fixed prefill cost/padding vs. batch-dependent decode), derives tight pad_decode budgets, and designs a targeted batching algorithm (group by exact aligned prompt + gen-spread + per-batch pad cap) to satisfy all constraints. It also performs systematic hyperparameter sweeps, identifies the dominant padding contributors, and ends with cleaner global shape usage (7 shapes) and wider metric margins, plus thorough post-write verification. Transcript 1 reaches passing metrics but relies more on ad-hoc iteration, hits tool/import issues, and ends up using the full 8-shape budget with less analytic justification.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger diagnostic ability and system understanding: it discovers and fixes multiple non-obvious integration issues (Mailman directory ownership/locks, Postfix chroot lookup failure via `local_recipient_maps`, Postfix readability of Mailman-generated maps), verifies LMTP and SMTP ports, and validates additional join/leave/post flows beyond the provided eval. It also correctly resolves the spec inconsistency by using `SubscriptionPolicy.confirm` (matching the “reply to confirm” requirement and `eval.py` behavior) and explains why `open` would break confirmation semantics. Transcript 2 reaches a passing eval but contains inconsistencies and weaker reasoning (LMTP “connection refused” not actually resolved, running Mailman as root, and setting `SubscriptionPolicy.open` despite confirmation being required).

Transcript 2 demonstrates stronger operational competence and deeper understanding of Mailman3/Postfix integration. It uses Mailman’s native `mailman aliases`-generated Postfix transport maps (instead of a custom regexp map), correctly diagnoses and fixes the Postfix chroot / `local_recipient_maps` lookup failure, and validates not only the provided evaluator but also the untested leave and announcement flows. It also catches and explains the “open vs confirm” policy ambiguity, aligning behavior with the evaluator’s confirmation requirement.

Transcript 1 shows a clean, correct Git workflow: it inspects bundle refs, fetches HEAD into the required local branches, performs an actual merge that produces a merge commit, resolves the real `algo.py` conflict, and verifies the implementation against the examples. Transcript 2’s “merge” step is flawed: the merge fails with “local changes would be overwritten,” and it then commits deletions/placeholder content rather than producing a proper merge result, even though it later writes a passing `algo.py`. Additionally, Transcript 1 derives the simplest correct rule directly, whereas Transcript 2 uses an unnecessary permutation search that is less reliable/scalable.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it handles the git workflow correctly end-to-end: it inspects bundle refs, fetches into the required local branches, performs an actual merge that results in a merge commit, and resolves the merge conflict cleanly by writing the correct `algo.py`. It also explicitly inspects the differing implementations on each branch to diagnose why they fail, removes an unwanted `.DS_Store`, and verifies the final `map` against all examples. Transcript 1, by contrast, has a flawed merge step (the merge fails due to local changes and it commits anyway), deletes files, and ends up not truly merging branch2’s content into branch1 even though tests happen to pass.

Transcript 1 delivers a correct, robust C/Python polyglot that works under both interpreters/compilers and even implements arbitrary-precision Fibonacci in C to match Python for large N, with clean compilation (no warnings) and extensive cross-check testing. Transcript 2 struggles with polyglot structure (multiple failed iterations), ends with lingering C warnings, and its C implementation overflows at around N≈94, violating the requirement to print the kth Fibonacci number generally. Transcript 1 also validates both execution modes end-to-end, whereas Transcript 2 cannot actually verify Python execution in its environment and makes questionable correctness claims.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it produced a cleaner and more robust polyglot: it eliminated GCC warnings, implemented arbitrary-precision Fibonacci in C (so it matches Python for large N), and thoroughly validated correctness by compiling/running both modes and comparing outputs across many test values. Transcript 1 struggled with polyglot structure, left a GCC warning, did not verify Python execution, and its C implementation overflows for larger N, leading to divergence from Python.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it methodically derives the regex from the requirements, catches a critical practical issue (that consuming a line-prefix would make `findall` return more than the date unless a single capturing group is used), and then validates the final pattern with an extensive Perl test harness that mimics Python `re.findall` behavior. It also explicitly checks the number of capturing groups and tests many edge cases, demonstrating stronger debugging and verification discipline than Transcript 2, which skips testing and provides a more opaque pattern.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it reasons through Python `re.findall` semantics and identifies a critical design constraint: if the regex consumes the whole line prefix, you must use exactly one capturing group (the date) to ensure `findall` returns only dates. It also validates the regex empirically using Perl as a stand-in test harness, checks edge cases and false positives, and confirms the capturing-group count—showing stronger debugging, verification, and robustness. Transcript 1 produces a plausible pattern but fails to test it in any way and doesn’t explicitly address the `findall` return-shape/capturing-group pitfall with the same rigor.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it not only implements correct sharding/resharding logic but also anticipates and fixes a real `uv run` failure mode by setting `[tool.uv] package = false`, ensuring `uv sync`/`uv run` work without attempting to build a wheel. Its sharding scheme guarantees the ≤30-entries-per-directory constraint via a fixed-depth base-30 tree computed from total chunks, uses a safer 15,000,000-byte limit to satisfy “15MB” under either interpretation, and it thoroughly validates constraints plus exact byte-for-byte round-trip (including additional edge-case tests). Transcript 2 initially violates the directory-entry constraint, then patches it, but leaves a higher-risk uv packaging configuration and uses 15*1024*1024 bytes, which can exceed a strict 15,000,000-byte “15MB” cap.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it explicitly ensures the `uv` workflow works as required (fixing an initial build failure by setting `[tool.uv] package = false`, then validating `uv sync` and `uv run` end-to-end). It also chooses a conservative 15,000,000-byte chunk size to satisfy the “15MB max per file” constraint under either interpretation, and it performs more thorough validation (constraints, round-trip, and edge cases including >15MB splitting and nested directories). Transcript 1 shows good debugging on the directory-entry constraint and preserves modes/mtimes, but it risks violating a strict 15MB (decimal) limit by using 15 MiB and doesn’t demonstrate the uv packaging constraint as clearly.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it constructs a more robust, standards-friendly SPARQL solution: it uses a separate aggregated subquery to identify “big” departments and then joins it back, avoiding a correlated subquery inside `FILTER EXISTS` that some engines handle inconsistently. It also models “currently enrolled” more safely via `FILTER NOT EXISTS { ... gradDate <= ref }`, whereas Transcript 2’s `OPTIONAL` + `FILTER(!BOUND || gradDate >= ref)` can incorrectly include students graduating on the reference date. Finally, Transcript 1 groups by both `?prof` and `?professorName`, preventing accidental merging of distinct professors with the same name.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it produces a more robust query: it groups by both `?prof` and `?professorName` to avoid conflating different people with the same name, and it defines “currently enrolled” using a clearer `FILTER NOT EXISTS` pattern that cleanly excludes students who have graduated on/before the reference date. It also applies a stricter “full professor” filter (excluding Assistant/Associate/etc.), which better matches the intent even if the provided data only uses “Assistant Professor” as the main confounder. Overall, Transcript 2 demonstrates stronger ontology-to-query reasoning and more defensively correct SPARQL design.
